opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I find really fascinating, because it gets at what selection actually means in evolutionary search. Classically, the selection operator is pretty dumb: you rank candidates by fitness, maybe add some novelty or diversity term, and keep the top performers. That works, but it throws away a lot of information. Fitness is a single scalar, and it says nothing about *why* a candidate is good or whether it's a promising stepping stone for something better later.

When you bring an LLM into the loop as a kind of meta-selector, you can give it much richer context. It can look at the code or the program that defines a candidate, the evaluation logs, the failure modes, and how that candidate relates to the rest of the archive. Then it can make a judgment call: this one scores a bit lower, but it's trying a structurally different idea that's worth exploring. Or: these three are basically the same trick with different hyperparameters, so let's not spend more budget on all of them. That's very close to what a human researcher does when they look at a set of experiments and decide what to follow up on.

That said, I'd be careful not to overclaim. A few things I think about a lot:

First, LLMs carry strong priors. That's a blessing because they know what tends to work, but it's also a curse because they can collapse diversity. If you let the model pick freely, it often gravitates toward the familiar, "textbook" solution, and you lose the open-endedness that makes evolutionary search valuable. So in practice I like hybrid schemes: keep a quality-diversity archive or some explicit novelty pressure as the backbone, and let the LLM act as an advisor or a reweighting mechanism on top, rather than replacing selection entirely.

Second, there's a cost question. Evaluations can be expensive, but so are LLM calls if you're doing them at every generation for every candidate. So you want the LLM to be used where its judgment adds the most, for example deciding which parents to mutate or which branches of the tree to expand, not re-ranking things that a cheap metric already sorts well.

Third, calibration and reward hacking. If the LLM is reading evaluation outputs, it can be fooled by candidates that look good superficially. You still need ground-truth evaluation to be the final arbiter. The LLM should help you allocate search effort, not define what success is.

So the way I frame it: the LLM becomes a learned, context-aware prior over where to search next. It's sort of like going from a fixed heuristic to something closer to a research intuition. And I think the really exciting direction is when that intuition itself improves over the course of the run, when the system learns from its own history which kinds of bets paid off. That's where it starts to feel less like hyperparameter tuning and more like automated scientific discovery.

r001.rationale: The response describes the LLM as a meta-selector, advisor, and learned prior, but does not frame it as a surrogate model.

r002.rationale: It discusses the cost of frequent LLM calls, but does not say that raw programs and fitness evaluations quickly exhaust the LLM’s context capacity.

r003.rationale: It suggests giving the LLM code, logs, and archive context, but does not state that evolutionary search information needs to be compressed for prioritization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought a lot about with the evolutionary model merging work at Sakana, and later with the AI Scientist stuff. The basic tension is that evolutionary search is incredibly sample-hungry, and every candidate you evaluate costs you real compute, especially when the candidates are full models you have to run on a benchmark. So the question becomes: can you use a language model as a kind of prior, or a heuristic, to decide where to spend your evaluation budget?

The way I think about it is that the LLM is basically acting as a surrogate for the fitness landscape, but a very different kind of surrogate than what you'd get from, say, a Gaussian process in Bayesian optimization. A GP only knows what it's seen in your run. An LLM comes in with this enormous amount of world knowledge about what architectures tend to work, what hyperparameter regimes are sensible, what kinds of merges have made sense in the past. So in the early stages of a search, when you have very little signal, that prior is worth a lot. It can tell you "these three candidates look like obvious dead ends, don't bother evaluating them" and you save a huge amount of compute.

But I'm also fairly cautious about it, and there are a couple of failure modes I worry about. The first is that LLMs are conservative by default. They'll push you toward things that look like what's already in their training data, and the whole point of evolutionary search is to find the weird, non-obvious solutions that a human wouldn't have proposed. If you let the LLM gate everything, you risk collapsing the diversity of your population, and diversity is really the engine of evolution. So in practice I like a hybrid: let the LLM propose or rank, but always reserve some fraction of the budget for random exploration or for candidates the LLM is skeptical about. That way you're hedging against the prior being wrong.

The second thing is calibration. The LLM will happily give you a confident ranking, but it has no real sense of how uncertain it is about any particular candidate. So you need to actually close the loop. You evaluate some of the candidates, you feed the results back into the context, and over time the model's judgments become grounded in your specific problem rather than just in general priors. That's actually one of the things I find most exciting here: the LLM can do a kind of in-context learning over the search history. You show it the lineage, the mutations that worked, the ones that didn't, and it starts to pick up on patterns that are very specific to your task. That's something a classic evolutionary algorithm is really bad at. It has no memory beyond the current population.

And then the last point, which I think is underrated, is that the LLM gives you interpretability almost for free. When it says "prioritize this one," it can also tell you why. Maybe the explanation is post hoc, maybe it's partially confabulated, but it gives the human in the loop something to react to. With a pure black-box evolutionary run you get a trajectory of fitness scores and not much else. So even if the LLM's prioritization is only modestly better than random in terms of raw sample efficiency, the fact that it can narrate the search is genuinely useful for the researcher.

So the short version: use it as a prior and a memory, not as a dictator. Keep the exploration pressure on, close the feedback loop so the model actually learns from your evaluations, and treat its explanations as hypotheses rather than ground truth.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes the LLM as “acting as a surrogate for the fitness landscape.”

r002.rationale: It does not say that supplying raw programs and fitness evaluations quickly exhausts the LLM’s context capacity.

r003.rationale: It discusses feeding search results and lineage back into the LLM, but does not state that this information needs to be compressed.

astra-6.text:
I think of the LLM as a proposal mechanism. In an evolutionary search, you have a population of candidates, you evaluate them, and then you use that feedback to decide what to try next. The LLM can help make that decision more informed: given the models we’ve tried and their performance, which modifications look promising, and which candidates should we spend compute on?

The distinction I’d make is between proposing something promising and knowing that it’s good. You still need to evaluate it. A model can give a very convincing explanation for why an architecture should work, but that explanation isn’t a fitness measurement.

And you want to preserve exploration. If you always prioritize what the LLM finds plausible, you might keep rediscovering familiar architectures. So I’d mix its suggestions with mutations that don’t depend on its judgment, and then ask whether that guidance actually helps us find better models under the same evaluation budget.

r001.rationale: It describes the LLM as a proposal mechanism that suggests promising candidates, but does not frame it as a surrogate model.

r002.rationale: It does not mention raw programs, fitness evaluations, or context capacity being exhausted.

r003.rationale: It does not state that search information needs to be compressed for the LLM.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the LLM as a proposal mechanism. In an evolutionary search, you have a population of candidates, you evaluate them, and then you have to decide what to try next. An LLM can look at the candidates and their fitness scores and suggest which ones are worth modifying, or which ideas might be worth combining.

The interesting question is whether it gives you a useful prior over that search space. Can it recognize some structure that would otherwise take many evaluations to discover? But you still need the evaluation loop. A model can give a very convincing explanation for why a particular architecture should work, and that explanation might have very little relationship to its actual performance.

So I would let it influence where you spend your compute, while keeping some exploration independent of its recommendations. Then you can ask a concrete question: with the same evaluation budget, do you find better models than you would with a simpler selection strategy?
